A1.notes.Q3: I see grades as academic data, but Absalon tracking feels like surveillance. Sensitive data should only help fairness, not just boost accuracy.
A1.notes.Q4: Trust is built on transparency. I cannot explain a 'black box' to a distressed student; I need clear reasons to be helpful.
A1.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student is worse than over-contacting some. We must ensure marginalized groups are not overlooked by the model.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored; personal invites build rapport. Early intervention is key, so continuous monitoring is better than annual checks.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic info, err on the side of caution. But for personalized contact, I'd rather miss one than risk intruding unnecessarily on a student's life.
A1.Q8.1: Students must have the right to opt-out of the model entirely without penalty or stigma affecting their studies.

A2.notes.Q3: Academic data is vital, but Absalon tracking feels invasive without clear benefit. Sensitive demographics should never drive predictions directly, though they might help balance fairness if handled strictly.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is our currency in advising. If I cannot explain why a student was flagged, they won't trust the advice or feel safe coming to me.
A2.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is worse than contacting some unnecessarily. However, we must ensure minority groups aren't systematically overlooked by the model's blind spots.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach shows care. Twice a year balances urgency with not overwhelming students. Continuous monitoring feels like surveillance; periodic check-ins feel supportive.
A2.notes.Q7: General emails can be mass-distributed safely. Personalized messages require advisor time, so we risk fewer contacts there, but better to over-include slightly in that high-touch mode.
A2.Q8.1: The biggest concern is the 'black box' effect eroding the human relationship between student and advisor. We must ensure the model remains a tool for conversation, not a verdict.

A3.notes.Q3: I see value in performance data for early signs, but login tracking feels like surveillance unless the gain is huge. I would never use sensitive traits to predict difficulty.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is built on transparency. If I can't explain why a student was flagged, they won't trust the support offered. A 'black box' is unacceptable for human interaction.
A3.notes.Q5: We cannot afford to miss marginalized students who already struggle more. Equalizing recall ensures we catch those most at risk, even if it means some false positives in other groups.
A3.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored. A personalized note referencing specific course struggles, followed by a voluntary meeting, works best. Waiting for annual checks is too late.
A3.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's better to reach too many than miss one in need. For personalized outreach involving staff time, we must be more precise to avoid overburdening students.
A3.Q8.1: Students need to control their own data. A 'dashboard' where they can see what the system knows about them and opt-out of non-essential tracking would build essential trust.

S1.notes.Q3: I don't want the university watching my every login click. That feels like surveillance, not support. Grades are fine to improve accuracy, but demographics should never be used.
S1.notes.Q4: If I get a warning, I need to know why so I can fix it. Black box models are too scary; if you can't explain it, don't use it.
S1.notes.Q5: I was missed by the system last time because I didn't fail many credits immediately but just slowed down. It is vital to catch everyone, even if it means a few false alarms.
S1.notes.Q6: Don't spam me constantly. A gentle, anonymous email with an option to meet is best. Too much contact feels aggressive when I'm already stressed.
S1.notes.Q7: For generic info, it's better to miss no one and get a few annoyed emails. But for personal messages from an advisor, I'd rather be missed than have my privacy invaded wrongly.
S1.Q8.1: Please ensure there is a clear, easy way to opt out completely if a student feels the system is watching them too closely.

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student, I am wary of using my data for profiling beyond academic metrics. Course performance is logical; Absalon tracking feels like surveillance. Sensitive demographics must be strictly excluded to prevent bias against non-EU students.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to trust the system. A 'black box' algorithm is too dangerous; if it can't explain itself clearly, I prefer not using it over a complex one with unknown logic.
S2.notes.Q5: As someone from outside the EU, I fear models trained on Danish data might miss international student struggles (lower recall). It is better to help slightly fewer people overall than to systematically ignore those who need it most.
S2.notes.Q6: I prefer a gentle, non-intrusive email first, with an option to talk if needed. Constant surveillance-style contact is stressful. Twice a year feels respectful of my autonomy and privacy.
S2.notes.Q7: For generic info, missing a few isn't terrible, but flooding everyone with irrelevant messages creates noise. For personalized advice, precision is key because it feels more invasive; we must balance support vs. privacy carefully.
S2.Q8.1: The survey assumes all students struggle similarly to Danish peers. International students face unique hurdles (language, isolation) that standard credit data might not capture until too late. The model needs context-specific training or human oversight.

S3.notes.Q3: Using Absalon data feels like surveillance; I track my own login to manage stress, not to be judged by algorithms. My disability data must never be used for scoring.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm contacted to trust the advice. If an advisor can't explain it, how can they help me solve my specific problem?
S3.notes.Q5: Missing students with non-traditional paths is worse than false alarms. We need to ensure marginalized groups aren't left behind by 'average' performance metrics.
S3.notes.Q6: A voluntary meeting is less intrusive than a phone call or personalized email which assumes I am failing. Check-ins should be regular but low-pressure.
S3.notes.Q7: General emails are okay to send to many. Personalized messages feel more invasive, so we must be careful not to over-contact students who might just need time.
S3.Q8.1: Students with chronic illnesses often need flexibility that looks like 'failure' in standard metrics. The model shouldn't penalize reduced course loads which are a legal accommodation.

S4.notes.Q3: Using Absalon data feels like surveillance, but my ADHD made me fail without realizing it until too late. However, high school GPA and demographics feel invasive and irrelevant to current struggles.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to understand *why* I was flagged to trust the support. If the AI is a black box, it feels like a judgment without accountability. Explainability is crucial for dignity.
S4.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help hurts more than contacting those who don't. But we must ensure neurodivergent and marginalized students aren't left behind by a model trained on 'normal' study patterns.
S4.notes.Q6: A generic email is easy to ignore, especially with executive dysfunction. I need a personal invitation to talk to an advisor who actually understands my situation before I hit a wall.
S4.notes.Q7: Better to send an unnecessary email than miss someone silently struggling. However, too many false alarms with personalized messages might feel patronizing or create anxiety if not handled well.
S4.Q8.1: The model must be trained on data that includes neurodivergent students who succeeded later. If it only learns from standard trajectories, it will flag us as 'risky' when we are actually just different learners.

S5.notes.Q3: Using grades is fine, but tracking my Absalon logins feels like surveillance. As an international student, I fear my background data could bias the model against me unless used strictly to fix fairness.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the advice. If it's a black box, I might ignore it or feel anxious about being judged without reason.
S5.notes.Q5: Missing international students because they study differently is dangerous. We often lack the informal networks locals have, so we need to be found even if it means contacting some who don't need help.
S5.notes.Q6: A cold personalized email might feel intrusive, but a general invite to talk is helpful. Waiting once a year is too slow; help should be immediate when issues arise.
S5.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's safer to over-notify so no one slips through cracks. For personalized messages involving an advisor's time and my dignity, I prefer a stricter balance.
S5.Q8.1: The survey misses the language barrier aspect. As a non-native speaker, my grades or activity might look 'risky' simply because I process academic texts slower, not because I lack competence. The model must account for this to avoid false positives.

S6.notes.Q3: I dropped out before; I know early signs matter. But tracking my LMS clicks or nationality feels like surveillance, not care. Data must prove huge benefit to justify privacy risks.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know WHY I'm flagged. If a black box tells me I might fail, I feel helpless and suspicious. Transparency builds trust.
S6.notes.Q5: As an international student, being missed by the system is worse than a false alarm. We need equal chances to be found when struggling, even if it means fewer total hits.
S6.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored. A personal note from an advisor that mentions specific struggles (e.g., language or credit count) makes it real. Catch me early, don't wait for the end of term.
S6.notes.Q7: A generic email is harmless if sent to one too many people; missing a struggling student is costly. With personalized outreach, we must be careful not to overwhelm or stigmatize.
S6.Q8.1: The model might miss students who are 'quietly failing' because they work hard but struggle with the language or culture, even if their grades look okay at first glance until it's too late.

S7.notes.Q3: As a dyslexic student, I see value in activity data if it catches silent struggles early. However, detailed logs feel like surveillance. Disability status should only be used to ensure the model doesn't fail students like me.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the support offered. A 'black box' feels dangerous, especially when my disability might be misinterpreted as lack of effort by an unexplainable algorithm.
S7.notes.Q5: Missing a student in need is worse than contacting one who doesn't need it immediately. Models often fail students with non-standard learning needs, so prioritizing equal recall for all groups is crucial.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. I need a conversation with an advisor who understands that struggling doesn't mean failing. Early, continuous support is key before crises happen.
S7.notes.Q7: Better to check in too often than wait until it's too late. The embarrassment of a wrong flag is minor compared to the risk of dropping out unnoticed.
S7.Q8.1: The model must be trained on data from students with disabilities. If not, it will likely flag my struggles as anomalies rather than predictable patterns requiring support.

S8.notes.Q3: I dropped out once, so I know data matters for prevention. But tracking my every click on Absalon feels like surveillance. Grades are okay; detailed activity logs feel invasive.
S8.notes.Q4: As a former dropout, if I get flagged without knowing why, I'll feel judged, not helped. I need to understand the reason to trust the support.
S8.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is worse than contacting a few extra people. We must prioritize catching those at risk, even if it slightly reduces overall efficiency or fairness metrics.
S8.notes.Q6: A voluntary meeting is best; it feels supportive, not punitive. Early intervention works if the student feels safe asking for help immediately.
S8.notes.Q7: Generic emails are low stakes, so casting a wide net is fine. Personalized messages feel heavy; I'd prefer to miss some cases than have the university assume too much about my situation.
S8.Q8.1: The system must ensure that being flagged doesn't appear on permanent records or affect future admissions/employment. The fear of being 'labeled' prevents many from seeking help.

S9.notes.Q3: Using grades is fine, but high school data feels intrusive for a Master's student. I absolutely cannot accept the university tracking my mental health status or disability details to flag me; that breaches trust.
S9.notes.Q4: As someone who has struggled to explain my delays due to health, I need clear reasons. If an algorithm flags me without a logical explanation I can understand and challenge, I feel powerless.
S9.notes.Q5: We cannot afford to miss students in the most vulnerable groups, like international students or those with disabilities. It is better to contact a few extra non-needy students than to leave someone struggling alone.
S9.notes.Q6: A generic email feels cold. A personalized note showing someone understands my specific context, followed by a voluntary meeting, would feel supportive rather than surveilling.
S9.notes.Q7: For general info emails, casting a wide net is fine. But for personalized messages that mention my situation, I prefer high accuracy to avoid the stigma of being wrongly targeted.
S9.Q8.1: The system must have a human review step before any contact. An algorithm making mistakes about mental health could cause real harm if not checked by a real person who understands context.
